blocks.text: Prompt engineering is the practice of crafting the input given to a language model, the wording, structure, examples, and constraints, so that the model produces the specific kind of output you actually need, without changing anything about the model itself.

This topic covers what prompt engineering actually is at its core, why the exact same model can produce dramatically different results from two different inputs, and how this skill relates to the other techniques for shaping model behavior covered later in this course.
1. The Same Model, Two Different Outputs

blocks.alt: The same pretrained model produces a weak output from a vague input but a strong output from an engineered input

blocks.text: A single pretrained model, with its weights never changing, can produce a vague, unhelpful answer to one input and a precise, genuinely useful answer to a differently worded input asking for essentially the same thing, this gap is exactly what prompt engineering exists to close.
2. Prompt Engineering as Translating Intent

blocks.alt: A user goal is translated through prompt design into specific model behavior

blocks.text: At its core, prompt engineering is the skill of translating what you actually want, your real goal, into the specific input structure that reliably steers a language model toward producing it, a model has no access to your intent beyond what the prompt itself communicates.
3. The Building Blocks of a Prompt

blocks.alt: Word choice, structure, examples, and constraints all combine into an effective prompt

blocks.text: Effective prompts are built from several combinable elements, precise word choice, a clear structure separating different kinds of content, illustrative examples, and explicit constraints on the output, later topics in this module cover each of these elements in much greater depth.
4. Prompt Engineering vs Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Prompt engineering makes no weight changes, fine tuning changes model weights

blocks.text: Prompt engineering shapes behavior entirely through the input text, with the underlying model weights never changing, fine tuning, covered in a separate course, actually adjusts the model weights through additional training, prompt engineering is generally faster to iterate on and requires no training infrastructure at all.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","What Changes"],"rows":[["Prompt engineering","Only the input text given to the model"],["Fine tuning","The model weights themselves, through additional training"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Prompt Engineering Is Iterative

blocks.alt: A draft prompt gets tested, then refined, then tested again in a loop

blocks.text: A first attempt at a prompt rarely produces the ideal output immediately, prompt engineering in practice is a loop, draft a prompt, test the actual output against real inputs, refine the wording or structure based on what went wrong, and repeat until the output reliably meets the requirement.

code.content:
prompt_v1 = "Summarize this article."
# Output too generic, missing length and tone guidance

prompt_v2 = (
    "Summarize the following article in 3 bullet points. "
    "Use a neutral, factual tone. Do not include opinions."
)
# Output now consistently matches the actual requirement

blocks.text: 6. Where Prompt Engineering Sits in an Application

blocks.alt: A raw user request passes through a prompt engineering layer before reaching the LLM and producing application output

blocks.text: In a real application, prompt engineering usually lives as a layer between the raw user request and the model call itself, taking a user simple question and wrapping it with system instructions, formatting requirements, and relevant context before it ever reaches the model.

blocks.title: This layer is often invisible to the end user
blocks.content: A user typing a simple question into a chat interface rarely sees the actual prompt sent to the model, the application has usually already added instructions, examples, and formatting rules behind the scenes.

blocks.text: 7. Does Prompt Engineering Still Matter as Models Improve?

blocks.alt: Older weaker models needed heavy prompt crafting, newer stronger models still need clear intent communicated

blocks.text: Stronger models genuinely need less elaborate prompt crafting to get a reasonable result than older, weaker models did, but even the most capable model still cannot read your mind, clearly communicating format, tone, and scope requirements remains necessary, the skill shifts from compensating for model weakness to precisely specifying genuine requirements.

blocks.title: This shift is why the skill has not disappeared
blocks.content: As models have improved, prompt engineering has moved away from tricks that compensate for a weak model and toward clearly and completely specifying what a genuinely capable model actually needs to know to do the task correctly.

blocks.text: 8. The Skills This Course Builds On This Foundation

The rest of this course builds directly on this foundation, prompting techniques like few-shot examples and role prompting, structured output formatting, system prompt design, and prompt optimization all extend this same core idea, deliberately shaping the input to reliably shape the output.
9. Prompt Engineering Is a Practical, Testable Skill

Unlike some areas of machine learning that require deep mathematical background, prompt engineering is directly testable by anyone with access to a model, you can try a prompt, observe the actual output, and refine it, this hands on, empirical quality is part of why it has become such a widely practiced skill.
Worked Example

A developer building a customer support tool sends the prompt "Answer the customer question" to a model, along with the raw customer message, the response comes back inconsistent, sometimes too long, sometimes missing key details, sometimes using an inappropriately casual tone.

After applying prompt engineering, adding a system instruction specifying tone, a required response length, and an explicit structure for including relevant policy details, the same underlying model now produces consistent, appropriately toned responses across a wide range of customer questions, with no change to the model itself.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming a vague, underspecified prompt should produce a precise output without the model being told what precise actually means here
Treating prompt engineering as a one time task instead of an iterative process informed by actual output review
Reaching for fine tuning immediately when a well engineered prompt would solve the problem faster and more cheaply
Writing a prompt without ever testing it against a range of realistic inputs, only the one example that happened to work

blocks.text: Practice

Take a task you would want a language model to help with, write a first, minimal prompt for it, run it, then identify one specific way the output falls short and rewrite the prompt to address exactly that gap.
Key Takeaway

Prompt engineering shapes a language model output entirely through the input text, without changing the model itself, making it a fast, iterative, directly testable skill for translating a real goal into the specific instructions a model needs to reliably produce it.
